title: Scientists Smash 30-Year Record for Superconductors at Normal Pressure!
summary: What if electricity could travel without losing any energy? That's the dream of superconductors—materials that let electricity flow with zero resistance. But there's a catch: most superconductors only work at super-cold temperatures, colder than outer space! Now, scientists at the University of Houston have broken a record that stood for over 30 years. They created a superconductor that works at -122°C (151 Kelvin) at normal pressure—no squeezing needed! That's still really cold, but it's a big step toward making superconductors practical. The old record was -140°C, set in 1993. The new material is 18 degrees warmer. That might not sound like much, but in the world of superconductors, it's huge. The team used a trick called pressure quenching. First, they squeezed the material under super high pressure to boost its superconducting powers. Then, while keeping it cold, they suddenly released the pressure. The material kept its improved abilities even at normal pressure—like a memory of being squeezed. Why does this matter? Today, about 8% of electricity is lost as heat when it travels through power lines. Superconductors could save billions of dollars and reduce pollution. They could also make MRI machines cheaper, help build fusion reactors, and create ultrafast electronics. The researchers, led by Ching-Wu Chu and Liangzi Deng, published their work in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Chu was part of the team that discovered a famous superconductor in 1987, so he's a legend in this field. Room temperature (about 25°C) is still far off, but this new record shows we're getting closer. Maybe one day, we'll have power lines that never waste energy—and that would be super cool!
why_it_matters: If superconductors work at higher temperatures, we could have power lines that never waste energy, meaning cleaner air and cheaper electricity for your home and school.

background_read: Superconductors are materials that can carry electricity perfectly, with zero waste. But for over a century, we could only use them at super-cold temperatures, often needing expensive liquid helium.

The previous record for a superconductor working at normal pressure was set in 1993 at -140°C. Breaking that record after 30 years is a big deal because even a small temperature bump makes future technology more practical.

MRI machines in hospitals already use superconductors, but they still need special cooling systems. If scientists can make superconductors work at higher temperatures, MRIs could become much cheaper and available in more places.

Ching-Wu Chu (a physics professor at the University of Houston) and Liangzi Deng are famous for pushing superconducting temperatures upward. Chu was on the team that discovered a superconducting ceramic in 1987, which jump-started the race for higher-temperature superconductors.

WHERE: In a laboratory at the University of Houston
WHY: To move closer to room-temperature superconductors that could save energy, money, and help the environment

perspectives.description: They are excited because even an 18-degree improvement is a huge step. It shows we are slowly climbing toward a world where superconducting wires could be wrapped around cities.
Some say -122°C is still far from room temperature, so it might take decades before we see everyday uses. We need more breakthroughs.
This record proves that the pressure quenching method works well, but maybe other tricks, like new materials, will be needed to finally reach room temperature.
